name: BodyTite

lead: BodyTite is a radiofrequency-assisted liposuction system from InMode. It removes fat and heats the tissue so the skin tightens, aiming at a leaner contour with less loose skin than liposuction alone. It is used on the abdomen, flanks, arms and thighs.

A probe under the skin delivers bipolar RF energy that liquefies fat and heats surrounding tissue with temperature monitoring, and the fat is then aspirated. Published reports describe it as filling a gap between liposuction and excisional surgery such as brachioplasty or abdominoplasty. Evidence is mostly surgeon-authored series and retrospective reviews, plus small registered studies.

paras: It is a surgical procedure performed by a surgeon, typically under local or general anesthesia, followed by a recovery period with compression and swelling that settles over weeks. Final contour is judged once swelling resolves.

Reported effects include swelling, bruising and numbness, with burns, infection, seroma, hematoma and asymmetry described as less common. A 97-patient series reported major complications in 6.25% of patients per one summary. US FDA clearance covers electrocoagulation and hemostasis rather than body contouring as such.

angle.text: BodyTite removes fat while tightening the overlying skin, for a leaner contour with less loose skin than liposuction alone. RF energy liquefies fat before it is aspirated and heats the skin so it contracts. The contour change is the result of the procedure; evidence is mostly surgeon-reported series.

lead: BodyTite is a radiofrequency-assisted liposuction (RFAL) system made by InMode. A probe placed beneath the skin delivers bipolar radiofrequency energy to liquefy fat and heat the tissue, after which the fat is aspirated; the heating is intended to make the skin contract, addressing laxity that liposuction alone may leave.[1][2] It sits within the wider family of energy-assisted liposuction methods that also includes ultrasound-assisted and laser-assisted techniques.[3]

The appearance goal is a leaner, tighter contour in one session: liposuction removes the fat, while the radiofrequency heating is meant to make the overlying skin shrink back so that it does not hang or ripple afterwards. People most often seek it for upper-arm, abdominal, flank and thigh contours, and some for the lower face and neck through the smaller FaceTite and AccuTite devices from the same family.[4][5]

It is used for body areas such as the abdomen, flanks, arms and thighs, and published reports describe it as filling a treatment gap between liposuction and excisional surgery such as brachioplasty or abdominoplasty.[4][6] Evidence consists mainly of surgeon-authored case series and retrospective reviews, with a small number of registered studies.

According to Grokipedia, the InMode RF System received US FDA 510(k) clearance (K163190) in December 2016 for electrocoagulation and hemostasis in dermatological and general surgical procedures, rather than for body contouring as such.[1]

paras: A 2018 supplement describes RFAL as a relatively new energy-assisted body contouring concept, using the BodyTite device to apply electromagnetic energy to soft tissue during suction lipectomy to produce soft tissue contraction.[4] Per Grokipedia, bipolar energy flows between an internal electrode in the cannula and an external electrode on the skin, with temperature and impedance monitoring intended to limit thermal injury.[1]

In the technique as described in the surgical literature, the procedure is carried out under local tumescent anaesthesia, with the internal probe moved beneath the skin to deliver heat to the fat layer and to the underside of the dermis before fat is suctioned out. Surgeons who use it describe the endpoint as a target skin temperature and a drop in resistance read from the device, rather than a fixed time, and attribute the later tightening to collagen contraction and remodelling in the heated layer over the following months.[4][1] Because the energy is delivered inside the tissue instead of through the skin surface, proponents contrast it with non-invasive devices that heat from the outside.[5]

Liposuction removes fat through a cannula attached to suction. Variants include tumescent, power-assisted, water-jet, ultrasound-assisted and laser-assisted techniques, and radiofrequency-assisted liposuction is listed among them as using radio waves to melt fat and possibly tighten skin.[3] The modern technique traces to the mid-1970s work of Arpad and Giorgio Fischer in Rome, to Yves-Gerard Illouz's extension of it across the body, and to Jeffrey Klein's tumescent method in the 1980s, which allowed local anaesthesia.[3] Wikipedia reports that by 2015 liposuction had overtaken breast augmentation as the most common cosmetic procedure in the United States.[3]

Standard liposuction removes volume but does not by itself tighten the skin, which is why surgeons have looked for adjuncts that cause the skin to contract. BodyTite belongs to that group: the same session that removes fat also heats the underside of the skin and the tissue between, with the aim of a smoother, firmer contour.[4]

Reports describe use on the upper arms, where adding RFAL to liposuction was proposed to induce skin contraction in patients who might otherwise be recommended brachioplasty, with its visible scar.[7][8][6] A 2019 paper combined adjustable-depth fractional radiofrequency with bipolar radiofrequency for skin laxity in patients described as lying in a treatment gap.[9] A 2025 paper reports endotissutal bipolar radiofrequency for facial changes associated with weight-loss medication, sometimes called Ozempic face.[10]

A 2022 review of energy-based devices in male body contouring describes such devices as extending the indications of conventional procedures, using heat to destroy fat or tighten soft tissue, with a stated advantage of improved outcomes without an increase in scar burden, and notes that patient selection and education are central to satisfaction.[11]

A 2010 safety and feasibility study evaluated a novel radiofrequency-assisted liposuction technique.[12] A 2012 prospective series reported 97 patients treated under local anesthesia, at a time when the device was described as awaiting FDA approval,[2] and another 2012 series treated overweight patients for reshaping and tightening.[13] A 2012 upper-arm report described adding RFAL to liposuction.[7]

A 2023 report described BodyTite for upper arm lifting,[8] and a 2022 review covers nonexcisional arm contouring.[6] A 2024 retrospective review compared Renuvion helium plasma radiofrequency with BodyTite bipolar radiofrequency after liposuction or body contouring.[14] A registered retrospective evaluation of 10 participants examined treatment of cellulite of laxity.[15] Grokipedia summarises figures from some of these reports, including major complications in 6.25% and minor complications in 8.3% of the 97-patient series.[1] Studies are generally small and largely surgeon-authored.

The 2022 arm-contouring comparison is a randomised controlled study, and the earlier feasibility work included 97 patients under local anaesthesia and 17 women treated for aesthetic reshaping and skin tightening.[6][2][13]

Published reports are mostly case series. In the first feasibility series, 23 subjects had BodyTite treatment of the hips and lower abdomen between July and December 2008; the procedure was completed in all, aspirated volume averaged about 2.4 litres, operative time averaged about 158 minutes, and weight and circumference reductions were significant at 6 weeks and 3 months, with skin tightening judged optimal by the surgeon in every patient and no severe systemic or local complications.[12] The authors called for a larger sample and for comparison with conventional and other energy-assisted liposuction.[12]

A randomised study of arm contouring compared three approaches in 176 patients treated between 2017 and 2020: ultrasound-assisted liposuction followed by BodyTite radiofrequency (53 patients), the same liposuction followed by Renuvion helium subdermal coagulation (66 patients), and ultrasound-assisted liposuction alone (57 patients). At a minimum of six months, 96 patients (80.6 percent) in the energy-treated groups reported satisfaction and an independent plastic surgeon rated results good to excellent in 97 of 119 cases; the authors concluded that nonexcisional arm contouring can be extended to difficult cases of laxity with energy-based devices.[6]

Surgeons who use RFAL describe a ceiling: the technique is intended for mild-to-moderate laxity, and when the excess skin is large, excisional surgery such as brachioplasty or abdominoplasty remains the reference approach in the literature.[4][6]

Grokipedia lists swelling, bruising, numbness and tenderness as common effects, and burns, infection, seroma, hematoma and asymmetry as less common. It also states that FDA adverse event reports cite isolated cases of third-degree burns and cellulitis, and lists pregnancy, active infection and implanted electronic devices as contraindications.[1] Grokipedia itself notes that much of its sourcing is clinic marketing, so its statements are not independently verified here.

For liposuction generally, Wikipedia lists deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation, bleeding, infection, fat embolism, seroma, altered sensation, skin necrosis and contour irregularities among reported complications, with risk rising as the volume removed increases; burns are noted as a concern with ultrasound devices.[3] Energy-assisted methods add the possibility of thermal injury, which is why the device monitors temperature and impedance.[1]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and cosmetic culture
paras: BodyTite is mostly discussed as a clinic procedure rather than a do-it-yourself measure. People interested in a leaner jawline, neck, arms or abdomen encounter it as a minimally invasive alternative to excisional lifts, and the smaller-area siblings FaceTite and AccuTite are marketed for the lower face and neck.[5] The pitch in clinic materials and the surgical literature is the same: less scarring than a lift and some skin tightening, with the limits of what a skin-contraction device can do set by how much laxity there is to begin with.[4][6]

InMode, founded in 2008 by Moshe Mizrahy and Dr Michael Kreindel according to Grokipedia, developed the platform, with Dr Stephen Mulholland associated with early RFAL work.[1] The RF System obtained FDA clearance in December 2016, and a 40W configuration (K171593) followed in 2017, per the same source.[1] Smaller-area siblings include AccuTite and FaceTite.[5]

Early reports in 2008 to 2010 evaluated the system as a novel radiofrequency-assisted liposuction technique, and a 2012 series described it while the device was awaiting FDA approval, which places the first clinical experience well before the 2016 clearance.[12][2] Later publications extended the approach to the upper arms, the male torso, the breast envelope, post-weight-loss facial changes and combination protocols with helium plasma, reflecting its use beyond the original abdominal indications.[7][8][14][10]

timeline.event: First clinical series of 23 subjects treated with BodyTite, published in 2010. [12]
Safety and feasibility study of RFAL published.[12]
Series of 97 patients under local anesthesia published; device described as awaiting FDA approval.[2]
InMode RF System receives FDA 510(k) clearance K163190 (December).[1]
Supplement reviewing RFAL soft tissue contraction published.[4]
